paragraphs: I am Leo, and I am a big fan of cartoons. In my opinion, a good picture says more than a long text. Lily does not agree with me. She writes for our class blog, and she loves words. "Words tell the day and the time," she says. "A poster is only a picture," she says. "A poster is a story in one look," I say.

On Thursday, Teacher Kim asked for a notice about the next trip on the old town trail. "Who can make one?" she asked. "I can," Lily and I said at the same time. Lily wrote ten lines with the day, the time, and the things to bring. I drew a big green flag with a paw print and a boy with a backpack. Under the picture, I wrote only three words: "TRAIL TRIP, SATURDAY."

"I like both notices," said Teacher Kim. "I will print both." But the printer in the library was not available. Teacher Nick's class used it for their math test. We waited at the desk for ten minutes. A guy from Tom's class stood next to us. "Cool boy with the backpack!" he said when he saw my picture. "Are you a fan of cartoons too?" I asked him. "Of course," he said.

At last, Teacher Kim put both notices on the board near the library door. Mine was on the left, and Lily's was on the right. At lunch, I stood in the hall and counted the children. Twenty children stopped at my poster, but only four stopped at Lily's text. "I told you," I said to Lily. Lily did not say anything. She only said, "Count again after the next break."

After the break, I counted again and watched more carefully. Fourteen of the twenty children looked at my poster and then at Lily's text. They wanted to know the time. "Anyway, my poster brings them to your text," I said. "And your text gives them the time," said Lily with a smile. Lily took a photo of the board for a post on our blog. That evening, I sent the photo to my grandmother. "I cannot read the small words," she wrote, "but I understand your picture." I am still a fan of pictures, and I am her youngest grandchild.
